name: Sulbutiamine

lead: Sulbutiamine is a synthetic compound made of two thiamine (vitamin B1) units, designed to be fat-soluble so it enters the body and brain more readily. People take it for more energy, motivation and mental stamina, which supports staying consistent with training and routines.

Servier has marketed it in France since 1973 as Arcalion for asthenia. After absorption it is reduced to thiamine, and rodent and cell studies show it raises thiamine phosphate levels, including in brain tissue. Human data come from small studies, including an uncontrolled trial in multiple sclerosis fatigue.

paras: Taken as an oral supplement, typically in the morning, and used as an energy or mental-stamina aid. Many users take it only occasionally rather than every day because of tolerance.

Trials mostly report headache and stomach discomfort at high doses. Daily use can lead to tolerance and paradoxical drowsiness. Other reports include diarrhea, insomnia, constipation and vertigo. It is not FDA-approved as a drug and appears on a US Department of Defense prohibited supplement list.

angle.text: Sulbutiamine is taken for less fatigue and more energy and motivation, which helps people keep up their training and routines. It is prescribed for asthenia in France; human data are sparse and no appearance outcome has been studied.

lead: Sulbutiamine (isobutyrylthiamine disulfide) is a synthetic, lipophilic derivative of thiamine (vitamin B1) in which two modified thiamine units are linked by a disulfide bridge [1]. Servier marketed it in France from 1973 as Arcalion, where it is prescribed for asthenia, a state of weakness and fatigue [1]. It is also sold in many places as a dietary supplement and used by some people as a nootropic and as an ingredient in stimulant and pre-workout style products [1][2].

Its place in a looks-focused wiki is through the recovery and energy chain: people use it hoping for less fatigue and better drive, which they connect to more consistent training, sleep routines and self-presentation, and so indirectly to physique and overall appearance. No study has measured a direct effect on appearance.

Research consists of a small number of mostly French and Indian clinical studies on fatigue, depression-related inhibition and cognition, plus animal and cell work on how it raises thiamine derivatives in the brain. A 2020 review described its history and literature and called for randomized controlled trials, noting that only a limited number of studies were done over five decades [3].

paras: In France sulbutiamine is prescribed for asthenia, and similar products are sold in other countries, including Russia under the name Enerion [1][4]. Wikipedia reports that in Uruguay it is prescribed for thiamine deficiency, asthenia, overwork, apathy, depressive states, memory disorders and certain wakefulness disorders [1]. Trials have also examined it for post-infectious fatigue, fatigue accompanying infections, inhibition in depression, and as an add-on in early Alzheimer disease [5][6][7][8].

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and supplement communities
paras: Forum users describe it as a stimulant or mood-and-motivation supplement, often combined with caffeine, choline sources or other nootropics. Some report feeling more social or energised, and others report brain fog after continued use. Commercial pre-workout and stimulant products have listed it among their ingredients. Sports researchers have discussed it as a sport supplement and, in some authors view, a possible masking strategy, and monitored its presence in doping-control urine samples [9][3].

The molecule is a dimer: the thiazolium rings of two thiamine molecules are opened, the hydroxyethyl groups are esterified with isobutyric acid, and the units are joined by a disulfide bond. This makes it far more fat-soluble than thiamine [1][2]. Its formula is C32H46N8O6S2 [1].

After absorption it is reduced to thiamine by thiols such as cysteine or glutathione [1]. In cultured neuroblastoma cells its uptake was unsaturable and about 20 times faster than that of thiamine, which uses a high-affinity carrier, and the compound was rapidly converted to free thiamine [10]. Injection in rats raised thiamine triphosphate in tissues [11]. Reviews also describe effects on cholinergic and glutamatergic transmission and, per Grokipedia, dopaminergic signalling, offered as explanations for the reported anti-fatigue and nootropic effects [3][2]. Studies in mice reported improved long-term memory formation, with possible cholinergic mediation [12], and a rodent object-recognition study reported memory improvements with chronic treatment [13].

Wikipedia describes it as hydrophobic, so it passes easily from the intestine into the bloodstream, where cysteine or glutathione reduce it to thiamine. It gives an elimination half-life of about 5 hours with renal excretion, and notes a 2014 review suggesting it may raise brain thiamine phosphate levels more effectively than benfotiamine and fursultiamine, which it says has not been fully verified [1].

Wikipedia reports that Japanese researchers in the 1950s, seeking thiamine derivatives with better bioavailability and using allicin from garlic as a model, produced sulbutiamine along with fursultiamine and benfotiamine [1]. A 2020 review places development of sulbutiamine in Japan in the mid-1960s, originally for thiamine deficiency (beriberi) [3][2]. Servier launched it in France as Arcalion in 1973 [1].

Wikipedia notes that a French validation procedure in the 1980s found no data supporting its use for fatigue, and that in January 1989 the 100 mg tablets were discontinued in favour of 200 mg tablets [1]. Over time the indication settled on asthenia, and a nootropic and sport-supplement market grew around it [1][3].

A randomized, double-blind trial in 326 general-practice patients with chronic post-infectious fatigue compared two doses of sulbutiamine with placebo over 28 days [8]. An eight-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in inpatients with major depression on clomipramine assessed psycho-behavioural inhibition and disability scales when sulbutiamine was added [7].

In an uncontrolled, observational study of 1,772 patients in India with infectious disease and asthenic symptoms, 51.7 percent had complete resolution of asthenic symptoms after 15 days of sulbutiamine added to anti-infective treatment, and side effects occurred in 0.6 percent; response was greater in acute infection [6]. In a multicentre randomized trial in early-stage Alzheimer disease, adding sulbutiamine to a cholinesterase inhibitor was associated with improved episodic memory and daily-life activities compared with entry scores [5].

A 2026 randomized trial of 450 children with primary nocturnal enuresis compared sulbutiamine, imipramine and the combination over six months; the mean time to successful therapy was shorter with sulbutiamine (3.2 months) than with imipramine alone [14]. A registration for the same question is listed [15]. Wikipedia also reports a 2017 uncontrolled trial in multiple sclerosis fatigue, and that it is unclear whether it affects drowsiness [1]. A Russian review concluded efficacy and safety in asthenia [4], while the 2020 review concluded that more randomized trials are needed [3]. No randomized trial has examined sulbutiamine for appearance.

Headache and gastrointestinal discomfort at high doses are most reported, with tolerance and paradoxical drowsiness described with daily use; diarrhea, insomnia, constipation and vertigo have also been noted [1]. In the Indian observational study side effects were reported in 0.6 percent of patients [6].

It is a prescription medicine in France and some other countries and a supplement ingredient elsewhere [1]. Grokipedia reports it is not FDA-approved as a drug and that it appears on a US Department of Defense list of prohibited dietary supplement ingredients [2]. Sports-science papers discuss it in anti-doping contexts [9].
Laboratory work has examined protection of retinal ganglion cells [16], anticancer applications [17] and diabetic nephropathy and diabetes-related testicular dysfunction in rodents [18][19].

lore.intro: On T Nation's 'Brain Function Boosters' threads, sulbutiamine appears in lists of nootropics, often alongside racetams and choline sources.[20][21] Appearance-related interest is indirect, through energy and motivation for training and social presentation.
